note.text:
Two lines on a flat surface (a plane) either meet or never meet.
• Parallel lines never meet, however far you extend them, like the two rails of a railway. We write (d) // (d′).
• Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle (90°), like the corner of your exercise book. We write (d) ⊥ (d′).
• Orthogonal also means 'at a right angle'. In a plane, orthogonal lines and perpendicular lines are the same thing.

Properties of lines in a plane:
• Through a point not on (d), there is exactly one line parallel to (d) and exactly one line perpendicular to (d).
• If (d₁) // (d₂) and (d₂) // (d₃), then (d₁) // (d₃).
• If (d₁) ⊥ (d₃) and (d₂) ⊥ (d₃), then (d₁) // (d₂).
• If (d₁) // (d₂) and (d₃) ⊥ (d₁), then (d₃) ⊥ (d₂).

worked_example.problem: (L) ⊥ (M) and (N) ⊥ (M). What can you say about (L) and (N)? A fourth line (K) is perpendicular to (L): what can you say about (K) and (N)?
steps: (L) and (N) are both perpendicular to the same line, (M).
Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel: (L) {lineRule(r1, r2)} (N).
(K) ⊥ (L) and (L) // (N). A line perpendicular to one of two parallel lines is perpendicular to the other: (K) {lineRule(lineRule(r1, r2), '⊥')} (N).

cards.idea: Parallel lines never meet, however far you extend them. We write (d) // (d′).
example: The two long edges of your ruler are parallel.

cards.idea: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. We write (d) ⊥ (d′). Orthogonal also means 'at a right angle': in a plane, orthogonal lines and perpendicular lines are the same.
example: The two edges at a corner of your exercise book are perpendicular.

check.prompt: Two lines in a plane {f.d}. They are:

misconceptions.explain: Parallel lines never meet. Perpendicular (orthogonal) lines meet at a right angle.

solution: Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular (orthogonal) lines meet at a right angle.

cards.idea: Through a point that is not on a line (d), there is exactly one line parallel to (d) and exactly one line perpendicular to (d).
example: Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.
A line perpendicular to one of two parallel lines is perpendicular to the other.

distractors.text: (d) and (d′) meet, but not at a right angle.

misconceptions.explain: // means parallel (never meet). ⊥ means perpendicular (meet at a right angle).

solution: // means parallel: the lines never meet. ⊥ means perpendicular: they meet at a right angle.

questions.prompt: ({X}) {r1} ({Y}) and ({Z}) {r2} ({X}). What can you say about ({Z}) and ({Y})?

distractors.text: Nothing can be said about ({Z}) and ({Y}).

misconceptions.explain: {r1 == '⊥' && r2 == '⊥' ? 'Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.' : r1 == '//' && r2 == '//' ? 'Two lines parallel to the same line are parallel.' : 'If two lines are parallel, a line perpendicular to one is perpendicular to the other.'}

solution: {r1 == '⊥' && r2 == '⊥' ? 'Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.' : r1 == '//' && r2 == '//' ? 'Two lines parallel to the same line are parallel.' : 'If two lines are parallel, a line perpendicular to one is perpendicular to the other.'}

questions.prompt: Through a point P that is not on the line (d), how many lines can you draw {which} to (d)?

misconceptions.explain: Through a point not on (d) there is exactly one {which} line to (d).
There is always exactly one: you can draw it with a set square and a ruler.

solution: Through a point not on (d) there is exactly one {which} line to (d).

questions.prompt: One of these deductions is false. Which one?

wrong.explain: Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel, not perpendicular.
A line perpendicular to one of two parallel lines is perpendicular to the other.
